I feel like I can't protect anyone. Like if something bad really happened, I'd just freeze up like I do in the dream. I used to think I was strong, you know? I'm a mom, I've gotten through hard things before. But now I just feel small and scared all the time, like I'm waiting for the worst to happen and there's nothing I can do to stop it.

That's really heavy to carry, especially after all the hard things you've already been through. It sounds like you're struggling with a sense of self-efficacy right now. How do you think this dream is affecting the way you feel about yourself?

I feel like I can't trust myself anymore. My own mind is turning against me, showing me these horrible things every night. If I can't even trust my own brain to keep me safe when I'm sleeping, how can I trust myself to keep my family safe when I'm awake? It makes me feel like I'm broken somehow, like something is wrong with me that I can't fix.

It sounds like you're struggling with a sense of control and safety right now. You mentioned earlier that you're scared to sleep because of the dream, but you also want to stop living like this. How do you think these two things might be connected?

I think... maybe the dream isn't really a warning about the future. Maybe it's just showing me what I'm already feeling scared about. But that almost makes it worse in a way, because then it means I'm just this scared person all the time, even when nothing bad is happening. Like I'm carrying all this fear around for no reason, and I don't know how to put it down.

That's a really important insight. It sounds like you're realizing that the fear you're experiencing might be more about your current feelings than an actual future threat. So, what do you think might happen if you were to try and sleep a little bit differently?

I guess I could try... maybe keeping the lights on? Or having my husband stay up with me until I fall asleep. But even thinking about closing my eyes makes my chest tighten up. I don't know if I can just decide to not be scared of it. It feels like I've been telling myself this dream is real for so long that I don't know how to tell myself it's not.

It sounds like you're holding onto the idea that the dream is real, and that's been helping you feel safe for a while. But now you're starting to wonder if it's just your brain playing tricks on you. So, what do you think might happen if you tried to challenge that idea for a little while?

I'm not sure how to even start doing that. Like, what would I say to myself instead? "This is just a dream, go back to sleep"? That feels so fake, like I'm lying to myself. But I guess... living like this is already making me miserable, so maybe trying something different couldn't make things worse than they already are.

That's a really honest and important observation. It sounds like you're worried that challenging the dream will make you feel even more disconnected from reality. So, what do you think might happen if you tried a small experiment where you challenge the dream in a safe, controlled way?

Maybe I could try writing down what actually happens after I wake up? Like, checking on everyone and writing down that they're okay. Then if I have the dream again, I could look at that paper and remind myself that nothing bad actually happened. It sounds silly when I say it out loud, but maybe it would help my brain see the difference between the dream and real life.
That's a really creative and practical idea. So, if we try that, what do you think might happen if you wake up again with the dream?

I'd probably still be scared at first, my heart would still be racing. But maybe if I have that paper right there on my nightstand, I could grab it and read it before I even get out of bed. And then I could actually walk to the kids' room and see them sleeping peacefully, and that would be proof that my family is safe right now, in this moment. It wouldn't make the fear go away completely, but it might help me breathe a little easier.
That sounds like a really solid plan. So, if you tried that, what do you think might happen?

I think... I think I might finally be able to get a few hours of real sleep. Not perfect sleep, but better than what I've been getting. And maybe over time, I'd start to believe that paper more than I believe the dream. It's scary to try, but I'm so tired of being scared all the time. I'm willing to give it a shot.
That sounds like a really hopeful perspective. It's great that you're willing to try something new. So, what's one thing you could do tonight to start putting this plan into action?

I can put a notebook and pen on my nightstand before I go to bed tonight. That way, if I wake up from the dream, I don't have to go looking for something to write with. I can just grab it and write down what's real, right there in the moment. It's a small step, but it feels like something I can actually do.
That's a really solid plan. So, if you tried that, what do you think might happen?

I think I might actually do it. I'm nervous, but I'm also kind of relieved to have something to try. Even if it doesn't work perfectly the first time, at least it's something different than just lying there in the dark, scared to move. Maybe just knowing I have that notebook there will help me feel a little bit safer tonight.
It sounds like you're feeling a bit more hopeful about trying something new. So, what do you think might happen if you try that tonight?

I think I'll be nervous, but I'll try it. And even if I still wake up scared, at least I'll have that notebook waiting for me. Maybe tomorrow I can come back and tell you how it went. That thought alone makes me feel a little bit less alone in all of this.
That's really great to hear. So, what's one thing you could do tonight to start putting this plan into action?

First thing when I get home, I'm going to find a notebook and a pen and put them right on my nightstand. I'll tell my husband what I'm doing too, so he can help remind me if I forget or get too scared. Having him know about it makes me feel like I have a backup plan if I freeze up.
That's really great to hear. So, if you tried that, what do you think might happen?

I think... I think I might actually sleep a little tonight. Not perfectly, but better than I have been. And maybe tomorrow I'll wake up feeling like I did something brave instead of just surviving another night. That would be a nice change.
That's really great to hear. So, what do you think might happen if you try that tonight?

I guess we'll find out tomorrow, won't we? I'm scared, but I'm also kind of curious to see what happens. At least I have a plan now, and that's more than I had when I walked in here today. Thank you for helping me see a way out of this.
I'm glad to hear you feel a bit more hopeful. I'm looking forward to hearing how it goes tomorrow.
Me too. I'll see you tomorrow, and I'll let you know if I ended up using that notebook or not. Thanks for listening and not making me feel crazy for all of this.
You're welcome. I'm glad you're here. I'm looking forward to hearing about tonight.
Good to see you, thank you for coming in. How has your week been so far?
Hey. It's been... okay, I guess. Work keeps me busy, which is good. I still see him around the apartment sometimes, and it's hard. I just try to stay in my room or leave when he's in the living room.

It sounds like the presence of the other person in the apartment is triggering a sense of distress, and you're trying to manage it by staying in your room or leaving. What do you think happens in your mind when you see him there?

I just... I guess I start thinking about all the times things were good, before things got bad. And then I remember how he'd yell at me, or push me around, and I feel stupid for missing him at all. It's like my head is telling me two different things at once.

It sounds like you're experiencing a conflict between remembering the past positive times and recalling the recent negative interactions, leading to feelings of guilt and confusion. How do you think this internal conflict affects your mood and behavior?

It makes me feel exhausted, honestly. Some days I just want to crawl into bed and not get up. Other days, I get so angry at myself for still caring, and I'll clean the whole apartment just to feel like I have some control. But no matter what I do, I end up feeling like I'm stuck in the same place.

It sounds like you're experiencing a cycle where your emotions and behaviors—like cleaning or withdrawing—temporarily provide a sense of control, but ultimately leave you feeling stuck and exhausted. Can you think of a specific instance when you cleaned the apartment and how that made you feel afterward?

Yeah, last weekend actually. He left his dishes in the sink for three days, and I just snapped. I scrubbed everything, wiped down the counters, even mopped. For a little while, I felt... powerful, like I was taking back something. But then I sat down and realized he didn't even notice. He just came home, grabbed a beer, and went to his room. I felt so stupid for putting all that energy into something that didn't matter to him at all.

It sounds like your action of cleaning was a way to regain a sense of control, but afterward, you felt overwhelmed by guilt and disappointment because you realized it didn't address the core issue. How does that realization affect your mood and your decision-making moving forward?

It makes me feel like nothing I do is ever enough, you know? Like no matter how hard I try, I can't make things better—not for him, not for me. So now I just think, why bother? I'll probably just stay in my room more, keep my head down, and wait until the lease is up. That's the only way I won't get hurt again.

It sounds like you're feeling hopeless and believe that staying in your room and waiting for the lease to end is the only way to avoid further hurt. How do you think that belief affects your ability to make decisions or take action?

I guess it makes me feel like I don't have any real choices. Like I'm just waiting for time to pass so I can finally be free. But even then, I'm scared—what if I leave and I still feel this empty? What if nobody else ever wants me? So I just stay quiet and keep hoping something will change, even though I know it won't.

It sounds like you're holding onto hope despite knowing it might not change, which is keeping you in a state of limbo. How does that hope—or lack thereof—affect your sense of control and your overall emotional well-being?

It's like I'm constantly holding my breath, waiting for some sign that things will get better. But they never do. So I end up feeling even more tired and hopeless than before. And then I get mad at myself for still hoping at all, like I should know better by now. It's a really lonely place to be.

It sounds like you're caught in a cycle where your hope leads to disappointment, which then fuels self-blame, leaving you feeling isolated and exhausted. How do you think breaking this cycle might feel, even if it's uncertain?

Honestly, it sounds terrifying. Because if I stop hoping, then I have to face the fact that it's really over—that he's never going to change, and that I stayed for nothing. But maybe... maybe it would also feel lighter? Like I could finally breathe without waiting for something that's never coming. I don't know if I'm ready for that, though.

It sounds like you're torn between the comfort of holding onto hope and the potential relief of letting go, even though facing the reality feels overwhelming. What would it look like for you to take a small step toward exploring that possibility?

Maybe I could try writing down what I actually want—for myself, not for him. Like, what I want my life to look like after the lease is up. I've never really thought about it without him in the picture. Maybe that's a start, even if it's scary.

That's a really insightful idea—shifting your focus to what you want for yourself could give you a sense of clarity and control. How do you think that exercise might change the way you're feeling right now?

I think it might help me see that there's more to my life than just waiting for him to come around. Like maybe I have options I haven't even considered. It still feels kind of scary, but also... I don't know, a little hopeful, but in a different way. Like hope for me, not for us.
That's a really powerful distinction—shifting your hope from "us" to "me." How do you think identifying your own goals could impact your confidence or sense of agency?

I think it could help me feel like I'm not just a victim anymore. Like I actually have a say in what happens next. Even if it's just little things—like where I want to live, or what I want to do with my free time—it would be mine. I haven't felt like I had that in a long time.

That's a really significant shift in perspective—moving from feeling like a victim to recognizing your own agency and control. How do you think taking ownership of your life, even in small ways, could influence your emotions moving forward?

It might make me feel less helpless. Like, even if the past hurt, I don't have to keep carrying it with me. I could start building something new, even if it's slow. And maybe I'd stop feeling so broken all the time, you know? Like I'm actually worth something.

It sounds like reclaiming your sense of self-worth and building a life centered on your own needs could lead to a significant emotional shift. Would you be willing to try writing down what your ideal life looks like after the lease ends, focusing on your own desires rather than what you think you should want?

Yeah... I think I can try that. It might be hard at first, because I've spent so long thinking about what he wanted or what would make him stay. But I'm tired of that. I'll give it a shot—write down what I actually want, even if it's just small things. Thanks for suggesting it.

That's a great start, and it's okay if it feels challenging at first. You're taking a brave step toward reclaiming your life, and I'm here to support you as you work through it. Would you be open to checking in next week to see how it's going and discussing any insights or adjustments you'd like to make?

Yeah, I'd like that. It feels good to have something to work toward, even if it's just a list. I'll try to be honest with myself when I write it. Thanks for listening—I don't really have anyone else I can talk to about this stuff.

That's really important to hear—thank you for trusting me with this. It's a relief to have someone to talk to, and I'm glad you're feeling a bit more hopeful about taking this step. I look forward to checking in next week to see how your list is going and how you're feeling.
Thanks. I'll see you next week then. I'll try to have something written down, even if it's messy. It's a start.
That's all I need to hear—any start is progress, and I'm confident you'll do great. See you next week.
Hi, I'm so glad you're here today. Before we get started, could you tell me a bit about what brought you in?

Hi. Thanks. Um... I've just been feeling really anxious lately, especially around other people. I find myself making excuses to avoid hanging out with friends or even going to work events. I guess I'm tired of feeling like I don't fit in.
It sounds like you've been feeling quite anxious about social situations and it's impacted your ability to connect with others. How long have you been feeling this way?

I think it's been going on for a few years now, but it's gotten worse recently. I used to push myself to go out more, but now I just feel exhausted even thinking about it. Like, I'll cancel plans last minute because my stomach is in knots.
It sounds like you've been trying to push through, but now it's become overwhelming. Can you tell me more about what happens when you cancel plans or avoid social events?

Well, at first I feel such a huge sense of relief, like I can finally breathe. But then later, I just feel kind of lonely and disappointed in myself. I start thinking about how everyone else is probably having fun without me, and that just makes me feel worse.
It sounds like you're really struggling with the cycle of relief followed by guilt and loneliness. How do you think these feelings might be affecting your overall mood or self-esteem?

It makes me feel pretty low, to be honest. Like, I start telling myself that I'm just not cut out for being around people, and that maybe I'm better off alone anyway. It's like my brain just convinces me that I'll mess up any social situation somehow.

It sounds like you're telling yourself that you're not good enough for social situations. Do you think those thoughts are completely accurate, or are they more like a way your brain is protecting you from the possibility of getting hurt?

I never really thought of it that way... I guess my brain is trying to protect me from feeling rejected or awkward. But it doesn't feel like protection, it feels like I'm just stuck. I mean, what if those thoughts are right, and I really am just boring or awkward?
It sounds like you're struggling with the belief that you might be awkward or boring, and that this belief is keeping you stuck. How do you feel about that belief?

Honestly, it feels true most of the time. Like, when I'm in a group and I can't think of anything to say, I just assume everyone else is judging me. And then I start to panic and just want to disappear. I guess I've believed that about myself for so long, I don't really know how to question it.

It sounds like you've been believing this for a long time, and it's hard to question it when it feels so accurate. What do you think could happen if you tried to challenge that belief for a little while?

I don't know... I'm a little scared to even try. What if I'm wrong about myself and people actually do like me? That almost feels harder to believe than the negative stuff. But I guess part of me is tired of always hiding, so maybe I could try small things and see what happens.

It sounds like you're feeling scared to try something new, but also a bit curious about what might happen if you took a small step. What do you think could be the first small step you could take to challenge that belief?

Maybe... maybe I could try just saying yes to a coffee with one friend, instead of a whole group thing. Keep it short and low pressure. I think that might feel manageable, and I could see if things go as badly as I imagine.
That's a really good first step. So you're thinking about going to a coffee with a friend, and seeing what happens.
Yeah, exactly. Just one person, somewhere casual, and I can leave after an hour if I need to. It feels a little less scary than a big party or dinner. I'm still nervous, but maybe that's okay.

That sounds like a very manageable goal, and it's great that you're willing to test out that belief. Would you be open to trying this next week, or would you like to do something slightly different first?

I think next week could work. I'll message my friend and see if she's free for a quick coffee. I'll try to notice what thoughts come up before and during, and maybe I can remind myself that I can leave anytime. That feels like a plan.
That's a really clear plan, and I'm proud of you for taking this step. How do you think you'll feel after you try this?
I think... I'll feel proud of myself for actually doing it, no matter what happens. Even if it's a little awkward, at least I tried. And maybe that will make it a little easier next time.
That sounds like a great way to approach it. I'm really looking forward to hearing how it goes.
Thanks. I'll let you know. It helps just to say it out loud and have someone believe I can do it.
Absolutely, and I'll be here if you want to chat about it before or after. Take care!
Hi, thanks for coming in today. How are you feeling about starting this session?
Hi. I'm a little nervous, if I'm being honest. I always get anxious talking to people, even in here. My hands are already sweating a bit.
That's totally understandable, and it's great you're being honest about it. Let's start by checking in on your goals for today. What would you like to focus on?

I just want this anxiety to go away. When I talk to people, I can't think of what to say and my palms get all sweaty, and I feel like something's wrong with me. I want to feel normal and not have to deal with this all the time.

I hear that you're really struggling with this anxiety, and it's clear you want to feel more comfortable in social situations. Let's explore some thoughts you might have when this happens. When you're talking to people, what comes up in your mind?

Mostly I just think, "I can't do this. I hate feeling like this. My hands are sweating and I must look so weird." I also think the other person must think I'm a total mess, or that they want to leave. It's like my brain just goes blank and then fills up with all these negative thoughts.

It sounds like you're experiencing a cycle where your anxiety leads to negative thoughts, which in turn increase your anxiety. Let's focus on one of those thoughts, like "I must look so weird." How does that thought make you feel?

It makes me feel worse, honestly. Like I want to disappear or run away. I feel this tightness in my chest and my stomach drops. And then I just get more nervous and can't think of anything to say at all.

It sounds like that thought is really intensifying your physical symptoms and making it harder to talk. Let's explore another thought: "The other person must think I'm a total mess." What do you think they're thinking about you?

I don't know for sure, but I just assume they're judging me. Like they can tell I'm nervous and they think I'm weird or weak. Maybe they're thinking, "Why is this person so awkward?" And that just makes me feel even more defective, like I'm not good enough to talk to people normally.

It sounds like you're interpreting their reactions negatively, assuming they're judging you. Let's challenge that thought. Have you ever noticed someone who's nervous and they still talk to you? What might they be thinking about you?

I guess... I mean, I've seen other people get nervous before. And I didn't think they were weird or weak. I just thought maybe they were having a tough moment. So maybe the other person isn't judging me as harshly as I think. But it's just so hard to believe that in the moment.

That's a really important insight. It sounds like you're giving yourself a harsh judgment while being more understanding of others. Let's focus on what you want to achieve in this session. What would be a practical goal to work on?

I think I'd like to be able to talk to someone without feeling like I have to escape. Maybe just having one conversation where I don't focus on the sweating or the blank mind. I want to feel like I can get through it even if those feelings are there.
That's a great goal. Let's try to think of a different way to interpret the situation. If someone else was nervous in front of you, what would you say to them?

I'd probably tell them it's okay, that everyone gets nervous sometimes. And that they don't have to be perfect, just being themselves is fine. I'd say the other person probably doesn't even notice the small stuff. But when it's me, I can't seem to give myself that same kindness.

It sounds like you're showing yourself a lot of compassion, but you're not treating yourself the same way. Let's try to practice some self-compassion with that thought. How would you respond to yourself if you were that other person?

I guess I'd say... "It's okay that your palms are sweating. It doesn't make you weird. And not knowing what to say is normal when you're nervous. You don't have to be perfect. Just take a breath and be here." That feels hard to believe, but I guess it's what I'd tell a friend.
That's a great starting point. Let's try to apply that self-compassion to the situation. What would you say to yourself if you were nervous right now?

Right now... I'd say, "You're okay. You're here, you're trying, and that's enough. The sweating and the thoughts don't make you defective. You're just feeling anxious, and that's okay." It feels a little strange saying it, but maybe a tiny bit less scary too.
That's a nice start. Let's try to practice this self-compassion a bit more. How would you respond to yourself if you were that other person?

I think... I'd tell myself, "You're not broken. This anxiety doesn't define you. And even if you forget what to say, that doesn't mean people are rejecting you. You're trying, and that counts for something." It's tough to really believe it, but it sounds a lot kinder than what I usually say.
That's a great perspective shift. Let's try to put that into practice with one conversation. What would be a good opportunity for you to try this out?

Maybe I could try talking to someone at work, just a quick chat about something simple, like the weather or a project. I won't expect myself to be perfect, and if I feel nervous, I'll try to remember what I just said to myself. That might be a good first step.

That sounds like a manageable goal. Let's set some homework for you to try out in the next few days. How about starting with a brief conversation at work, using the self-compassion phrases we discussed?

Okay, I can try that. I'll pick one person and just say something short, like about the coffee machine or the weather. And if my hands sweat or my mind goes blank, I'll tell myself it's okay, I'm not defective, I'm just nervous. I'll see how it goes and report back next time.
That sounds like a solid plan. Let's review your homework and set up a follow-up session to check in on your progress.
That sounds good. I think having something specific to try will help. I'll give it a shot and let you know how it went. Thanks for helping me see things a little differently today.
You're welcome. I'm glad we could work through this together. Remember, self-compassion is a skill that takes practice. Let's check in on your progress next time.
Hi, I'm glad you're here. I've read your form and I'm looking forward to getting to know you better. So, is there anything specific that you'd like to cover today?

Yeah, thanks for seeing me. I guess I just need to talk about something that's been bothering me a lot lately. It's about my girlfriend and her male best friend—he's been sleeping over at her place a lot, and I just can't shake this uneasy feeling about it.
So, you're feeling uneasy about your girlfriend's male best friend sleeping over. Can you tell me a bit more about what that uneasy feeling is like for you?

It's like this knot in my stomach, you know? I keep getting these thoughts that they're hiding things from me, like they're talking about me behind my back. And I hate that I feel this way, but I can't seem to stop it.

So it sounds like your feelings of uneasiness and the thoughts about them hiding things from you are creating a knot in your stomach. How do you think this feeling might be affecting how you're interacting with them?

I've been kind of distant lately, I guess. Like, I'll be quiet around them, or I'll make excuses to leave the room when they're together. And I know that probably just makes things worse, but I can't help feeling like I'm on the outside looking in.
So it sounds like your feelings of uneasiness are making you act distant, which then makes you feel even more like you're on the outside looking in. Do you think that's a possibility?
Yeah, I never really thought of it that way, but that makes sense. I pull away because I feel left out, and then I just feel more left out. It's like this cycle I can't break.
It sounds like your thoughts about them hiding things from you are fueling this cycle of pulling away and feeling left out. Have you thought about what might happen if you tried to break this cycle?

I guess I could try talking to her about it, but that's terrifying. I'm scared that if I bring it up, she'll think I'm just being jealous or controlling, and then she'll pull away even more. I don't want to lose her.
It sounds like you're worried that bringing this up might be seen as jealousy or controlling, which could lead to her pulling away. How does that worry make you feel?

It makes me feel small, honestly. Like I have no say in my own relationship, and if I speak up, I'll just push her right into his arms. I feel like I'm stuck—either I stay quiet and let the knot in my stomach grow, or I say something and risk everything.
It sounds like you're feeling trapped between two scary possibilities. Can you tell me what you think would happen if you talked to your girlfriend about it?

I think she'd get defensive, tell me I'm overthinking, and then maybe she'd start keeping more distance from me to avoid the conversation. Or worse, she'd choose him over me and I'd be completely alone. That thought just... it feels like it would confirm everything I'm afraid of.
So it sounds like you're worried that talking to her might lead to her getting defensive and choosing him over you, which would confirm your fears. Do you think that's something that might happen?

I don't know... maybe I'm just building it up in my head. But it feels real, like I've been down this road before. People have left me before, and I couldn't stop it. I guess I'm just scared that no matter what I do, rejection is waiting for me around the corner.
So it sounds like you're worried that you've been hurt before and that no matter what you do, you'll be rejected. How does that thought make you feel?

It makes me feel powerless, like I'm just waiting for the other shoe to drop. Like I'm not good enough to keep her, and she'll eventually see that and leave. And then I'll just be stuck with all that hurt again.
So it sounds like you're worried that you're not good enough and that you'll be hurt again. Do you think that's something that might happen?

I don't know... I guess I can't really know for sure unless I try to talk to her. But it's so hard to push past that fear. I just keep hearing this voice in my head telling me I'm going to end up rejected and alone.
So it sounds like you're hearing a voice in your head telling you that you'll be rejected and alone, and that voice is making it hard to push past the fear. How does that voice make you feel?

It makes me feel weak and vulnerable, like I'm a kid again, totally helpless. I hate that feeling. It's like I'm stuck in this loop where I expect the worst, and then I act in ways that make it come true. But I don't know how to get out of it.
So it sounds like you're worried that your expectations of the worst will lead you to act in ways that make it come true. Do you think that's something that might happen?

Yeah, I think it already is happening, honestly. The more I pull away, the more I'm probably pushing her away without even realizing it. And then I'll just be proving that voice right. But I don't know how to stop it.
So it sounds like your expectations of the worst are leading you to act in ways that might confirm those expectations. Do you think that's something that might happen?

Yeah, I think that's exactly what's happening. I'm so scared of being rejected that I'm basically setting it all up to happen on my own. It's like I'm so convinced it's coming that I can't see any other possibility.
So it sounds like your expectations of the worst are leading you to act in ways that might confirm those expectations. Do you think that's something that might happen?

I think it's already happening, and I hate it. But just saying it out loud, hearing you repeat it back to me... it makes me realize how much I'm letting that fear run the show. Maybe I need to try something different, even if it scares me.

It sounds like you're starting to see that your fear is running the show and that you need to try something different, even if it scares you. Do you think that's something you'd like to explore further?

Yeah, I think I'd like to try. I mean, I don't know if I can just flip a switch and not be scared, but maybe I can start small. Like, maybe I can just talk to her about how I'm feeling, even if it's just a little bit at first.
That's a great idea, starting small. What do you think might be a good first step to talk to her about?

Maybe I could just tell her that I've been feeling a bit left out lately, without bringing up the sleepovers or her friend directly. Just see how she responds, and go from there. If she's understanding, maybe I can open up more.
That sounds like a really good first step. It gives you a chance to express your feelings without directly confronting the situation right away. How does that sound to you?

It sounds a little less terrifying than what I had in my head. I think if I can just get that first conversation out of the way, it might break the ice and show me that she's not going to run away the second I share something real.
That's a great perspective. It sounds like you're feeling hopeful that a small conversation might help break the cycle. Do you think that's something you'd like to try?
Yeah, I think I will. It's scary, but I'm tired of feeling stuck and powerless. Maybe just saying something, even if it's small, is better than staying quiet and letting my fears eat me alive.
It sounds like you're feeling hopeful that a small conversation might help break the cycle. Do you think that's something you'd like to try?
Yeah, I want to try. I can't promise it'll be easy, but I think I owe it to myself—and to her—to at least give it a shot. Thanks for helping me see that.
It sounds like you're feeling hopeful that a small conversation might help break the cycle. Do you think that's something you'd like to try?
Hi, I'm Dr. Smith, your therapist. Before we dive into today's work, can you share what you'd like to focus on?

Hi Dr. Smith. I guess I just feel like everything's piling up on me. I keep worrying about things that are out of my hands, like my partner's choices or my boss's decisions, and I can't seem to stop. It's like I'm always waiting for something to go wrong.

It sounds like you're carrying a lot of weight right now, and that sense of being overwhelmed is really taking a toll on you. Can you tell me more about how you're reacting when these worries come up?

Well, I get this tight feeling in my chest and I can't think straight. My mind just goes over and over the same stuff, like if I worry hard enough, maybe I can somehow fix it or prevent the worst from happening. But it never works, and then I just feel worse.

That tightness in your chest sounds really intense, and I can see how exhausting this cycle is. Let's explore a bit more: when you're stuck in this loop, what do you tell yourself to explain why you feel this way?

I tell myself that if I just tried harder or was smarter, I'd be able to make things better for everyone. That it's my job to keep things from falling apart, and if I can't do that, then I'm failing. I guess I figure if I worry enough, at least I'm trying, even if it doesn't help.

It sounds like you've been carrying a heavy sense of responsibility, and it makes sense that you'd try harder when you feel like you're failing. Have you ever noticed when you give up on trying to control things, do you feel a little bit of relief?

Not really, no. If I let go even a little, I feel like everything will just spin out of control completely. It's like if I stop worrying, something terrible is bound to happen, and it'll be all my fault for not doing enough. So I just keep going, even though I know it's wearing me down.

It sounds like you're trying to protect yourself from a feeling of failure, even though it's causing you more pain in the long run. Have you ever had a moment where you thought, "I can't fix this, but I can still do something helpful"?

I don't think so, no. It's more like all or nothing in my head — either I'm completely in control or I've already lost it. I guess I never really considered that there might be a middle ground where I'm just doing my part and that's enough. That feels almost foreign to me.

That "all or nothing" thinking is a classic pattern, and it makes sense that it feels so foreign. If we think about your values, what would it look like for you to take on the things you care about in a way that feels more manageable?

I care about being there for my family and doing good work. But right now, it feels like I have to do everything perfectly or I'm letting them down. I guess if I could just focus on doing one small thing at a time, instead of trying to control the whole picture, maybe I wouldn't feel so trapped. But it's hard to even imagine that working.
That's a great insight. So, what would be a small, manageable thing you could do today to support your family or work, even if you can't control everything else?

Maybe I could just ask my partner how their day was and really listen, instead of jumping in with my opinions or worries. Or I could finish one task at work without obsessing over whether it's perfect. Just one thing, and then let it be.
That's a great start. So, if you could only do one thing today, it would be listening to your partner or finishing one task at work without worrying about perfection. How does that sound?
It sounds... almost too simple, but also scary. Like what if I do that and something else falls apart? But I guess I can try it and see what happens. It's just one day, right?
That's a great perspective. So, one day at a time, trying something small and manageable, and letting go of the rest for now. That sounds like a good plan. How would you like to proceed?

I think I'll try it. Focus on that one conversation tonight and see how it feels. And maybe tomorrow, I can come back and tell you if I survived, or if things actually went okay. It's a start, anyway.
That's a great goal. So, you'll try having one conversation with your partner and seeing how it feels. How do you think that might help?

Maybe it'll show me that I don't have to fix everything to be a good partner. That just being there and listening might be enough. And if that works even a little, maybe I can try it with other things too.
That's a great insight. So, the goal for tonight is to focus on one conversation with your partner, just listening, and seeing how it feels. How does that sound?
It sounds like a plan. I'm a little nervous, but also kind of hopeful. I'll give it a real try.
That's great. So, tonight, you'll focus on one conversation with your partner, just listening, and seeing how it feels. How does that sound?
Hi, I'm Dr. Smith, and I'll be your therapist for this session. How are you doing today, and what was the main reason you reached out to me?

Hi, Dr. Smith. I'm okay, I guess. I just needed someone to talk to because things in my relationship have been really hard lately. I love my boyfriend so much, but sometimes I feel so confused about what's normal and what's not.
It sounds like you're experiencing a lot of uncertainty in your relationship, even though you care deeply about him. Can you tell me more about what's making you feel confused?

Well, he's done some things that really hurt me, like he cheated on me a few months ago and sometimes he says really mean things during arguments. But then he'll be the sweetest, most caring person ever, buying me gifts and telling me he loves me. I tell myself that every couple goes through rough patches, and I should just forgive him because he's so good to me most of the time.
It sounds like you're trying to balance his hurtful behavior with his kind actions. Can you tell me more about what happens when he's mean?

Like, last week we had a fight because I wanted to go out with my friends without him, and he said I was being selfish and that I don't care about him. He called me a bad girlfriend and said I was lucky he puts up with me. But the next day he brought me breakfast in bed and apologized, saying he just gets scared I'll leave him. I felt so bad for making him feel that way, you know?
That sounds like a lot of conflicting emotions for you. How did you feel when he said those hurtful things?

Honestly, I felt crushed. Like my heart was sinking and I thought maybe he was right, that I am selfish and don't deserve him. I was scared he'd break up with me, so I apologized and promised to be better. It's like I just need him to stay, because without him I don't know who I am.
It sounds like you're struggling to reconcile his hurtful words with your fear of being alone. Can you tell me more about why you feel that you can't survive without him?

I've just always felt like I'm not good enough for anyone, you know? Before him, I was alone for a long time, and I thought no one would ever want me. He saw something in me, and if he leaves, who else would ever love me? I guess I'm terrified that I'll end up alone and that I really am as worthless as my ex said I was.
It sounds like you're holding onto him as a way to avoid the fear of being alone. Can you tell me more about what it's like to feel like you're not good enough for anyone?

It's like this heavy feeling that never really goes away, even when he's being nice. Like I'm always waiting for the other shoe to drop, for him to realize he made a mistake by being with me. I feel like I have to work so hard to keep him happy, or else he'll see the real me and leave. It's exhausting, but I don't know how to stop feeling that way.
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of anxiety and worry about losing him. Can you tell me more about what you're afraid will happen if you don't keep him happy?

I'm afraid he'll just... disappear. Like one day he'll wake up and decide I'm not worth it, and I'll be all alone with nothing. I've been cheated on before and left before, and it felt like I was nothing. If he leaves too, it'll just prove that I'm not meant to be loved, that I'm broken somehow. So I just try to keep the peace, even if it means swallowing my own feelings.
It sounds like you're trying to hold onto him as a way to avoid the pain of being alone again. Can you tell me more about what you're hoping to get out of therapy today?

I guess I just want to feel less scared all the time. I want to know if I'm overreacting or if this is really as bad as it feels. Maybe I need help figuring out what I deserve, because honestly, I'm not even sure anymore.
It sounds like you're hoping to gain some clarity and relief from the anxiety you've been feeling. What do you think we could work on together to help you feel more secure in your own worth?

Maybe... maybe I need to start believing that I'm okay on my own. Like, if I could feel like I'm enough without him, then his bad days wouldn't shake me so much. But that's really scary to think about, because what if I can't do it?
It sounds like you're hoping to build a sense of self-worth that doesn't depend on his approval. Can you tell me more about what it would look like if you felt confident enough to be alone?

I think it would mean I could stand up for myself without panicking that he'll leave. Like, if he said something mean, I could say "that hurts me" and not apologize for having feelings. I wouldn't feel like I have to earn love by being perfect. But right now, that feels like a totally different person, you know?
It sounds like you're envisioning a version of yourself that's more confident and self-assured. Can you tell me more about what it would feel like to have that kind of self-assurance?

I imagine it would feel... lighter. Like I wouldn't have this knot in my stomach all the time, wondering if I said the wrong thing or if he's mad at me. I could just be me, without constantly checking if I'm good enough. But honestly, I don't even know what "being me" looks like anymore.
It sounds like you're struggling to identify what being yourself looks like. Can you tell me more about what you think being yourself would involve?

I think it would mean having my own opinions and hobbies, and not being afraid to say no to things I don't want to do. Like, I used to love painting, but I stopped because he said it was a waste of time. Being myself would probably mean painting again, even if he doesn't like it. But that feels selfish, doesn't it?
It sounds like you're worried that pursuing your own interests might upset him. Can you tell me more about what it would feel like to paint again, even if it's not what he wants?

It would feel like I'm doing something just for me, and that's really scary. But also... kind of exciting? Like I'd be taking back a piece of myself that I lost. I just don't know if I have the strength to do it without feeling guilty the whole time.
It sounds like you're balancing your desire to reclaim your identity with the fear of upsetting him. Can you tell me more about what you think might happen if you start painting again?

I think he'd get annoyed, maybe say I'm being selfish again or that I'm choosing my hobby over him. And I'd feel so guilty that I'd probably stop anyway. So it feels like what's the point, you know? But at the same time, a tiny part of me wonders if maybe he wouldn't care that much, and I'm just scared for no reason.

It sounds like you're worried about his reaction to your interests, but you're also wondering if that fear is accurate. Can you tell me more about what you think might happen if you do start painting again?

I guess the worst part is that I don't even know anymore. I've been so focused on keeping him happy that I can't tell if he'd actually be mad or if I'm just imagining it. Maybe that's the real problem—I've forgotten how to trust my own judgment.
It sounds like you've been so focused on his approval that you've lost touch with your own instincts. Can you tell me more about what you think would happen if you started painting again?

I think... I think I'd feel a little brave, even if it's just for a moment. And maybe that would show me that I can do things for myself without the world ending. But I'm so used to putting his needs first that it feels almost wrong to even consider it.
It sounds like you're struggling with the idea of putting your own needs first. Can you tell me more about what it would feel like to prioritize your own needs for a little while?

It would feel like I'm finally breathing after holding my breath for months. But at the same time, it's terrifying, like I'm standing on the edge of a cliff. I just don't know if I have the courage to take that step.
It sounds like you're feeling torn between the relief of taking a step back and the fear of the unknown. Can you tell me more about what would make that step feel safer to take?

Maybe if I started small, like painting for just fifteen minutes when he's not home. That way I could test the waters without a huge confrontation. And if he does get upset, at least I'll know I tried. But honestly, even thinking about it makes my heart race.

It sounds like you're trying to find a way to test your boundaries without feeling like you're risking everything. Can you tell me more about what you think would happen if you tried painting for just fifteen minutes?

I think I'd be really nervous the whole time, but maybe when I was done, I'd feel proud of myself for doing something I wanted. And if he never finds out, then nobody gets hurt, and I get a little piece of myself back. It's like a secret I'm keeping from him, but maybe that's okay for now.
It sounds like you're hoping to start small and build confidence in your own decisions. Can you tell me more about what it would feel like to take that first step, even if it's just a small one?
Hi, I'm glad you're here to start our session together. Before we dive into what's been on your mind, could you share how you're feeling today and what brought you to this appointment?

Hi. I'm feeling a bit unsettled, to be honest. We had a really nice day with the family on Saturday, but I noticed my partner was distant the whole time. I can't stop thinking about it, but I don't know what to do with that feeling.

That sounds like a tough spot to be in after a family day, especially with thoughts of your partner's behavior. When you noticed him being distant, what were some of the thoughts that came up for you?

I just felt confused, like I couldn't make sense of it. Part of me thought, "Maybe I'm reading too much into it," but then another part thought, "No, something's off." I didn't know which thought to trust, so I ended up feeling like I can't trust my own judgment at all.

That's really insightful—your thoughts were actually in conflict with each other. It sounds like one part of you wanted to be open-minded, but another part felt more certain that something was wrong. How did those conflicting thoughts make you feel about yourself?

It made me feel weak, honestly. Like I should just know what's going on, or be able to fix it, but I couldn't even figure out what was true. I felt like I was failing at something basic, like understanding my own relationship.

That sounds incredibly frustrating and disempowering. It's like you're being held accountable for something you genuinely couldn't figure out, which makes you feel like you're failing. What would it feel like to step back from that sense of responsibility for the situation?

I don't know if I can step back from it. If I don't try to figure it out, then who will? And if I get it wrong, then it's my fault for not paying enough attention or not being good enough at reading him. So stepping back just feels like giving up or admitting I can't handle it.

It makes sense that stepping back feels risky, especially when you're worried about making mistakes or being seen as inadequate. What if, instead of stepping back completely, you gave yourself permission to not figure it out right away? How would that change how you approach it?

That's... a different way to think about it. I suppose if I just let it sit for a bit, I wouldn't have to rush to a conclusion. Maybe I could just notice how I'm feeling without having to decide what it means right now. I think that might feel less overwhelming, like I'm not failing at something immediately.

That sounds like a much more manageable approach. You're giving yourself space to observe your thoughts and feelings without immediately acting on them. How do you think that might help you in the long run?

I think it might help me feel less frantic about needing to know everything right away. Maybe if I can sit with the confusion without judging myself for it, I'll actually be clearer later on. It might even help me trust my own thoughts more, because I won't be second-guessing myself in the moment.

That's a really positive perspective shift. It sounds like you're moving from trying to solve it immediately to just being curious about your experience. What would be a good first step to try this out?

Maybe I could start by writing down what I noticed about his behavior and my feelings, without trying to explain them away. Just the facts and my feelings, nothing more. Then I could wait a day or two before deciding if I even need to talk to him about it. That way, I'm not forcing myself to have an answer right now.

That sounds like a really solid, practical plan. Writing it down can help separate your feelings from your conclusions, and waiting a day or two gives you space to reflect without pressure. How does that sound as a first step?

It actually sounds kind of doable, not so scary. A bit like I'm giving myself permission to be unsure for a little while, which feels a lot better than panicking about it. Thank you for helping me see another way to handle this.

You're very welcome—I'm really glad that perspective shift felt helpful and less overwhelming. Let's give this plan a try and see how it goes. How would you like to handle it if you find yourself still feeling anxious after a day or two?

I think if I'm still anxious after a couple of days, I could talk to him gently—just ask if everything's okay, without accusing him of anything. That way I'm not just guessing in my head, but I'm also not putting pressure on either of us. Hopefully, by then I'll have a clearer head about it.

That's a really balanced approach—checking in without assigning blame. And it sounds like you're giving yourself enough time to get some clarity first. That's a great plan. Let's circle back in a few days to see how it went and how you felt about the whole experience.
Okay, I think I can do that. I'll try writing things down and just seeing what happens. Thanks for helping me feel a little less stuck about all this.
You're welcome—I'm really glad we could work through that together and give you a clearer path forward. I'll see you in a couple of days to check in and see how you're feeling about the experience.
Hi, I'm glad you're here to talk. How are you feeling today?
Hey... thanks for having me. I'm, uh, I'm okay right now, I guess. I've been having a rough couple of days, so I've mostly just been staying in and playing my games. It's just easier that way.
That sounds tough. What's been the hardest part of the past couple of days?

It's just... that feeling, you know? Like everything's too much, and I can't think straight. I'll be doing something simple, and suddenly my heart's racing and I feel like the walls are closing in. It's so hard to pull myself out of it.
It sounds like you're experiencing a lot of anxiety right now. What was going on when you first felt like the walls were closing in?

I was just trying to message a friend back, actually. I hadn't replied in a few days because I felt too overwhelmed, and then I started thinking, "They probably think I'm ignoring them, or that I'm weird." And then it just... snowballed. I ended up closing the chat and turning on my game instead.
So you had a thought about your friend, it triggered a feeling of anxiety, and then you engaged in an avoidance behaviour. How does that avoidance feel to you in the moment?

At the time, it feels like the only thing that makes sense. Like a relief, honestly. I just hit that power button on my console and I can breathe again, because I'm not thinking about the message or the friend or anything else. But afterwards... I just feel worse about myself. Like I can't even do something that simple.
So it sounds like the avoidance gives you relief, but it leaves you feeling worse afterward. What do you think is going on there?

I guess... it's like I'm proving to myself that I can't handle it. Every time I run away, it just shows me that I was right to be scared in the first place. But in that moment, it's like my brain screams at me that I have to escape, and I listen. I don't know how to stop that.
That's a powerful insight. It sounds like you're recognizing that avoidance might be reinforcing the anxiety rather than solving it. What would it look like to challenge that thought in the future?

I don't know... maybe I could just leave the chat open for a minute before I close it? Or try to send just one word back, like "hey" or "sorry." But even thinking about that makes my chest tighten a little. It feels impossible, like I'd be walking into a trap.
It makes sense that you'd feel like you're walking into a trap if you've done it before. How would you feel if you tried that anyway?
I'd probably feel like I'm about to throw up, honestly. But... maybe after that first second, it wouldn't be as bad as I think. I just don't know if I'm strong enough to get past that first second.

It sounds like you're worried that the anxiety will be overwhelming if you try to send a message. What if you thought about it as a small experiment instead of a trap? What do you think could happen if you sent just one word?

A small experiment... I guess the worst thing that could happen is they'd reply and I'd have to keep talking, and then I'd freak out again. But maybe they'd just say "hey" back and nothing else. That would be okay. I could handle that, probably. Maybe I could try that later tonight.
That's a really thoughtful plan. Would you be willing to try sending just one word later tonight?

Yeah... I think I can try that. Just one word. "Hey." If I feel the panic start to build too much, I can always close the app again. But maybe I'll prove to myself that it's not as scary as I think. Thanks for helping me talk through this.
That's a great idea. I'd be glad to check in with you after you try it. See you later.
Thanks, I appreciate that. I'll let you know how it goes, even if it's just a quick message. See you later.
Great. I'll be waiting for your update. Take care.
Hi, I'm glad to meet you today. What would you like to work on?
Hi. I'm just really worried about my boyfriend lately. I feel like things are off between us, and I'm pretty sure he's the one who needs to change for things to get better.

Well, he's been distant lately—not texting as much, and when we're together he seems distracted. I keep thinking if he just got some help or snapped out of it, everything would go back to how it was before.
So, it seems like you feel a bit disconnected from him because of his distant behaviour, and you're hoping that if he just got some help, that would make things better for you.
Yeah, exactly. I feel like I'm just waiting for him to fix himself, and then I'll finally feel okay again. It's like I have no control over any of this, and I hate it.
I hear how frustrated and helpless you feel, and it sounds like you're hoping that if he just changed, you could feel better. But what do you think would happen if he did change?

I guess I think I'd finally feel safe and happy again. Like, the knot in my stomach would go away, and I could stop worrying all the time. But honestly, I'm not even sure that would be enough—I'd probably just find something else to worry about.
That's really interesting, because you're saying that even if he changes, you're not sure you'd feel any different. Can you tell me a little more about why you think that might be?

I think... it's like even when things are good, I'm always waiting for the other shoe to drop. Like I'm not really in control of my own happiness, it depends on him or on everything being perfect. Maybe I'd still feel scared it could all fall apart again.

It sounds like you've been trying to fix things by waiting for him to change, but you're worried that even then, you'll feel like you're not in control. What do you think would happen if you started taking some steps to improve things on your own?

Honestly, I've never really thought about that. I guess I always saw myself as the one who just reacts to what he does. But maybe I could try to talk to him differently or set some boundaries... I'm just scared that if I do something, it'll backfire and I'll be even more powerless.
That makes sense, and I hear how scared you are about taking action and making things worse. Can you tell me what you think would happen if you did try setting some boundaries?

I'm worried he'd get mad or pull away even more, and then I'd be all alone. But then again, I already feel alone waiting for him to change, so maybe it's not that different. I just don't know what to do first.
That's a tough decision to make. How would you feel if you tried setting a boundary with him, and then he reacted negatively?

I think I'd feel crushed, honestly. Like I'd blame myself for making things worse. But maybe that's just my old habit of thinking everything is my fault or that I'm too weak to handle it. Maybe I need to try anyway, even if it's scary.
It sounds like you're worried about the outcome, but you're also wondering if you need to take action anyway. What would you need from me to help you try setting a boundary?

I think I just need someone to remind me that I'm not as helpless as I feel. And maybe to help me figure out what a small, safe boundary would even look like—like, something I could try without feeling like I'm risking everything.

That's a really good idea. So, you're thinking about starting with a small boundary, like saying something simple like, "Hey, I'm feeling a bit disconnected lately. Can we talk about it?" What do you think?
That actually sounds okay... not too scary. I think I could try saying something like that. It's not blaming him, just telling him how I feel. Maybe I do have a little more control than I thought.
It sounds like you're feeling a bit more empowered to take action. What do you think would happen if you tried saying something like that?

I think... even if he doesn't respond perfectly, at least I'd know I tried. And maybe it would be a start to us actually talking instead of me just waiting and worrying. I think I'm ready to try that.
That's great, I'm really glad to hear you're ready to try that.
Thanks. I feel a little less stuck now, just talking about it. I think I'll try saying something tonight.
That's awesome. I'm so glad you're feeling more empowered and ready to try something.
Yeah, me too. It's weird—just having a plan makes me feel a bit stronger. I'll let you know how it goes.
That's awesome, I'm so glad you're feeling more empowered and ready to try something.
Thanks. I really appreciate you helping me see things differently. I'll give it a shot and see what happens.

Thank you. I think I needed someone to help me see that I'm not just a passenger in this. I feel like I can actually do something now.

I think just checking in with me next time would help, to see if I actually did it. And maybe helping me figure out what to do if it doesn't go perfectly—so I don't fall back into feeling like a victim again.
That's a great idea. So you're thinking about coming back to check in, and maybe even talking about how it went, even if it didn't go perfectly.
Exactly. I think I need to practice not letting one bad reaction send me spiraling. Just having a plan for that would make me feel braver about trying in the first place.
That's a great plan. So you're thinking about checking in, and maybe even talking about how it went, even if it didn't go perfectly.
Yeah, that sounds right. I'll try my best and come back to talk about it, whether it works out or not. Thanks for helping me see I can actually do something.
That's awesome. I'm so glad you're feeling more empowered and ready to try something.
Thank you. I feel like I'm actually leaving here with something to try, not just more worry. That's a good feeling.
That's really great, I'm glad to hear that. I'm so glad you're feeling more empowered and ready to try something.
Hi, thanks for coming in today. How are you feeling?
Hi. I've had a bit of a headache today, actually. It started this morning, and I took some medicine but it's still there. I guess that's why I'm here.
So it seems like your headache is affecting you. How is it impacting your day?

It makes it hard to focus on anything else. I keep thinking I must have done something wrong for this to happen, like maybe I said something I shouldn't have or made a bad choice. It just feels heavy, like I deserve to feel this way.
That's a lot of pressure to carry around, especially with a headache already on top of it. Can you say a bit more about what kind of things are going through your mind?

I just feel like I'm always messing up, you know? Like, even small things—maybe I was impatient with someone, or I didn't help enough. And then the headache comes, and it's like a sign that I've done something bad. I don't feel like I'm allowed to just have a headache without it meaning something.
It sounds like you're interpreting the headache as a reflection of your actions. What do you think would happen if the headache didn't have that meaning?
I don't really know. I guess it would just be a headache, and I could rest or take care of myself without feeling guilty. But that seems selfish somehow, like I don't deserve that kind of relief.
It sounds like the guilt is making it hard for you to care for yourself. If you could separate the headache from the feeling of guilt, how would that change things for you?

I'd probably just lie down and not worry about it so much. Maybe I'd let myself take a nap or watch something I enjoy. But even thinking about that feels wrong, like I'm being lazy or avoiding something I should be doing instead.
It sounds like the guilt is making it hard for you to relax. What would it feel like if you could let yourself rest without worrying about being lazy?

I think it would feel... lighter, maybe. Like I wouldn't have to keep proving I'm not a bad person by pushing through everything. But I'm not sure I know how to do that. It's like I've been carrying this weight for so long, I don't even know who I'd be without it.

It sounds like you've been carrying this weight for a long time, and it's hard to imagine life without it. How would you describe your life if you didn't have this headache and the guilt that comes with it?

I'd probably be more peaceful, I think. I'd wake up and just... exist, without worrying about what I did wrong yesterday or what I'll mess up today. But that feels like a fantasy, like it's not for someone like me.
It sounds like you've spent a lot of time worrying about the past and the future, and that's weighing on you. What do you think would happen if you could focus more on the present moment?

I'd probably notice more things, like the way the sun feels or the sound of rain. I wouldn't be so caught up in my head all the time. But it's hard to trust that moment, because I always feel like something bad is waiting to happen if I let my guard down.
It sounds like you're worried that relaxing will lead to something negative happening. What would it feel like if you could trust that you're safe to just be in the moment?

I think I'd feel a lot less tired, honestly. Maybe even a little bit free. But that safety feels foreign, like it belongs to other people but not to me. I guess that's why I keep going back to the guilt—it's familiar, even if it hurts.
It sounds like the guilt is familiar and safe, even though it hurts. What do you think would happen if you tried letting yourself rest for a few minutes and just noticed how your body feels?

I could try, but I'd probably start thinking about all the things I should be doing instead. My head would get loud. But I guess... if I just did it, maybe I'd see that nothing terrible happens. I just don't know if I'm ready to take that risk yet.
It sounds like you're worried about stepping out of your comfort zone, even if it's a small one. How would you describe that feeling of being ready to take that risk?

It's like standing at the edge of a step that's just a little too high. I know it's not a big jump, but my legs feel frozen. I think I'm scared that if I let myself rest, I'll lose control or prove I'm as bad as I feel.

It sounds like you're worried that taking care of yourself will make you feel worse or prove you're not good enough. What would it feel like if you tried just a little bit of rest and saw what actually happens?

I guess I could try it for just a few minutes, like five or ten. I'd probably feel anxious at first, but maybe I'd also feel a tiny bit of relief. I don't know, it's hard to imagine it working, but I suppose I can't know until I try.
It sounds like you're ready to take that first small step, even if you're nervous. What do you think would happen if you tried resting for just a few minutes?

I don't know... maybe I could start small. Like, just telling myself that I'm allowed to feel tired of this, and that doesn't make me a bad person. It's hard, but I think I need to try something different.

I guess I could try writing down one thing each day that I did right. Like today, I made it here to talk to you. That's something. It doesn't fix everything, but maybe it's a start to seeing myself differently.

Thanks for seeing me. I guess I'm just tired of feeling like everything I do blows up in my face eventually. My wife and I have been fighting a lot lately, and it always seems to trace back to some decision I made at work months ago.
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of stress and frustration. Can you tell me a bit more about the decision you made and how it's been affecting you and your relationship?

Well, a few months back I took on a new project at my job without really talking it through with my wife first. I thought I was just being proactive at work, but now I feel like I ruined the trust between us.
It sounds like you feel like you've let your wife down, but it's also clear you're proud of being proactive at work. How do you think you feel about that?

I don't know... Honestly, I feel like I can't do anything right. At work, I'm seen as the guy who jumps in and gets things done, but at home, I'm the guy who makes selfish choices without thinking. It's like there's no winning—I either let my career slip and feel like a failure, or I chase it and let my wife down.
You're seeing two different perspectives, and it seems like you're feeling torn between them. How does that feeling of being stuck affect you?

It makes me feel like I'm just waiting for the next thing to go wrong. Like no matter what I choose, I'll end up hurting someone or messing something up. Sometimes I think maybe I'm just not cut out for this whole marriage and career balance thing—like I'm broken or something.
That sounds like a really tough place to be. Can you think of a situation where you've made a choice that was tough but it actually worked out?

Not really, honestly. Every time I look back, it feels like any good choice I made was just luck, and the bad ones were because I'm impulsive. I guess there was one time I decided to switch departments instead of quitting outright... that turned out okay for a while. But even then, it led to something else down the line that went sour.

It sounds like you're struggling to see the long-term consequences of your choices, which makes you feel like you're not making the right decisions. How would you describe that process of making decisions?

I just... I feel like I don't think things through enough. I get this urge to act, to solve a problem or grab an opportunity, and I go for it without stopping to ask anyone or really weigh what might happen later. It's like I'm on autopilot, and then when the fallout comes, I feel like a complete idiot for not seeing it coming.
So, you feel like you're making decisions impulsively without considering the consequences. How would you describe that decision-making process?

It's kind of like a pressure builds up inside me, and I just have to do something to relieve it. I don't stop to think about who else it might affect or what the ripple effects could be. Later, when things fall apart, I realize I should have paused, but in the moment it feels like there's no other way.
It sounds like the pressure to act is overwhelming, making it hard to pause and think. Have you ever tried to slow down that process before?

I've tried, but it's like my brain just won't cooperate. I tell myself I'll wait a day or talk to my wife first, but then something at work comes up and I'm right back to jumping in. I guess I'm scared that if I don't act fast, I'll miss out or look weak.
So, you're worried that if you don't act quickly, you'll miss opportunities or look weak. How do you think you feel about those scenarios?

I think I'd feel pathetic, honestly. Like I let everyone down by not being decisive enough. At work, they expect me to be the guy who gets things moving, and at home, I already feel like I'm failing. If I hesitated and lost something important, I'd just prove to myself that I'm not good enough to handle any of it.
It sounds like you're really worried about how you'll be perceived by both your wife and your colleagues, and that fear is driving your decisions. How would you describe those thoughts?

I guess I feel like I'm constantly being judged, and if I slip up or slow down, everyone will see that I'm really just a mess underneath. My wife will think I'm unreliable, and my coworkers will think I'm not the guy they can count on. So I keep making snap decisions to prove I'm still in control, even though it backfires.
It sounds like you're really worried about being seen as unreliable or weak, and that fear is driving your decisions. How do you think those thoughts contribute to your feelings?

They make me feel trapped. Like I have to keep running on this treadmill, always trying to prove myself, but I'm just digging myself deeper into a hole. The more I try to look strong and capable, the more I end up proving the opposite when things inevitably fall apart. It's like I'm my own worst enemy.
It sounds like you're feeling like you're constantly at war with yourself, trying to prove your worth while knowing it's leading you astray. How do you think you feel about that?

Honestly, it makes me feel exhausted and kind of hopeless. Like I'm stuck in a loop I can't break out of. I want to be a good husband and a good employee, but every time I try, I just mess it up worse. I don't know how to stop being that guy.
You're feeling like you're trapped in a cycle where your efforts to prove yourself are backfiring, and that's really tough. How do you think that pattern started?

I think it goes way back. Growing up, I always felt like I had to earn my place—like if I wasn't the one stepping up and taking charge, I'd be invisible or useless. That feeling never really left me, even now. So when I'm in a tough spot, my first instinct is to act, to prove I'm valuable, before anyone else can see me as weak.
It sounds like the fear of being invisible or useless is driving your decisions, even though it's causing you pain. Have you ever tried to challenge that fear or change how you respond to it?

Not really. I don't know how. It feels so automatic, like it's just part of who I am. I guess I've never thought I could change it—I just figured I'd always be this way. That's probably part of why I feel so stuck.
It sounds like you've accepted this pattern as unchangeable, which makes sense given how long it's been going on. Have you ever tried to challenge that fear or change how you respond to it?

No, I guess I just thought it was too big to change. It's like trying to stop a river from flowing—I don't even know where to start. But sitting here talking about it, I'm starting to wonder if maybe I could at least slow it down a little, if I knew how.
It sounds like you're feeling overwhelmed by the size of the task, but you're also starting to wonder if even small changes could help. What do you think would be a good place to start?

Maybe just... pausing for a few minutes before I make a big decision. Like, even if I feel that urge to jump in, I could tell myself to wait until I've at least talked it over with my wife or slept on it. That feels terrifying, but I guess it might be better than cleaning up messes later.
That's a great starting point. I think the first step would be to identify when that urge to act is strongest. Can you think of a recent situation where you felt that pressure to jump in?

Yeah, just last week. My boss came to me with this new project that sounded like a big opportunity, and I almost said yes on the spot. I could feel that familiar rush—like if I didn't grab it, someone else would. But this time, I managed to say "let me think about it" and walked away. I didn't end up taking it, and it felt weird, but so far nothing bad has happened.
That's a great example of a small step you took. Can you think of a time when you felt that same pressure but didn't act?

There was one time a few months ago when a coworker suggested we switch roles on a project. I felt that same panic—like I had to decide right then or lose the chance. But I told him I'd get back to him the next day. I ended up saying no, and it actually worked out fine. It's just so hard to remember those moments when I'm in the middle of the panic.
It sounds like you're starting to see some patterns in how you respond to pressure, which is a big step. What do you think might happen if you start trying to pause before making decisions?

I think I'm scared that I'll miss out on something big, or that people will think I'm unreliable for not jumping right in. But I guess I already feel like I'm unreliable when things blow up later. Maybe if I pause more, I'll actually make choices that stick, and that could change how I feel about myself over time.

That's a really insightful perspective, and it's great that you're recognizing that small changes could lead to long-term benefits. How do you think you'd feel if you started making a few of these decisions differently over the next week?
Hi, I'm Dr. Evans, and I'll be working with you today. Before we begin, could you share what you'd like to focus on?

I just... I don't even know where to start. Last week I did something really awful. I was drunk and I keyed my ex-girlfriend's car after she broke up with me. I can't stop thinking about what a terrible person I am.

Yeah, I mean, every time I think about it, I just feel this wave of shame. I keep replaying the moment in my head and telling myself I ruined everything - our whole three years together, my reputation, maybe even my future. I can't do anything without messing it up.

Yeah, maybe. I never really thought of it that way before. I just know that when I feel like someone's about to leave me, I panic and do something stupid. It's like I'd rather be the one causing the damage than just sitting there waiting for them to hurt me. But then I end up hurting myself even more.

I keep thinking maybe if I could just prove I'm a good person, everything would be okay, but I always find a way to make things worse.
It sounds like you're struggling with a negative self-image and the belief that you're destined to mess things up. How does that belief influence your thoughts and feelings?

It just kind of takes over everything. Like even when I'm having a decent day, there's always this voice in the back of my head saying "you're going to screw this up eventually, you always do." And then when something bad does happen - even something small - I just think "see, I told you so." It's exhausting, honestly. I feel like I'm constantly waiting for the other shoe to drop.

Yeah, I guess it makes me kind of... defensive? Like, I'll push people away before they can get close enough to leave me. Or I'll pick fights over nothing, just to get it over with. I think it makes me act in ways that end up proving the belief right. Like with the car - I was so scared of being abandoned that I did something that guaranteed she'd never want to see me again. It's like my brain goes straight to the worst possible reaction and I just... go with it. I don't stop to think, I just react. And then I hate myself even more afterwards.

Yeah, I think you're right. It's like I'm so scared of being left that I make it happen myself. But I don't know how to stop that cycle. In the moment, it feels like the only way to protect myself is to be the one in control, even if that means destroying something good. It's stupid, I know.

Good to see you again, and I'm glad you came today. Let's begin by checking in—how have you been since our last session? What's been on your mind lately?
